newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Paris bank mediator seeks hostage release.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Paris bank mediator seeks hostage release.

text.p: A government-appointed mediator on Tuesday called for the release of the chairman of Credit Foncier de France, held for the fifth day in a siege of the state-owned bank's headquarters by hundreds of staff.

But mediator Philippe Rouvillois said the release was not a pre-condition for the start of any negotiations with staff, who are protesting against a government plan to wind down the financially troubled property lender.

"I did not use the term pre-condition because that sounds like an ultimatum and I believe that the role of a conciliator is not to set ultimatums," Rouvillois said after he had met union representatives for an hour of talks.

"But in fact, I believe that it (the liberation) is a condition to allow a climate in which we can work fruitfully," he added. For the unions, Daniel Perrin said the talks were "brief but constructive".
Bank chairman Jerome Meysonnier and seven of his colleagues have been held in the bank offices since Friday afternoon.
"For the moment there's no question of a plan to end the occupation or holding of Meyssonnier," staff union representative Claude Dubeau told Reuters before the meeting.

French newspapers said that Prime Minister Alain Juppe's decision to intervene and appoint a mediator could break the deadlock with unions fighting government plans to shut down the property loans bank. But Dubeau said that was premature.

About three hundred people were occupying the central lobby of the plush Paris headquarters early on Tuesday, many of them having spent the night there sprawled across the marble floor of the giant atrium in sleeping bags.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announced in July that part of the debt-laden group would be spun off to another cooperatively run group called Credit Immobilier, which would take on 1,500 of the staff, with the rest shunted into a new state holding company that would be closed down gradually.

But he is now facing blanket media coverage of the plight of some 3,300 staff at a time of record unemployment and the thorny task of sorting out a bank which was set up by Emperor Napoleon III 145 years ago and has a long history of providing low-cost housing loans to France's poorer families.

After a fourth night sleeping in his office, Meyssonnier, who initially took a conciliatory line but said on Monday he considered himself a hostage, faced another day of mediation talks which were expected to drag on for some time.

More than a thousand staff took part in the occupation on Monday, with employees pouring in from around the country to keep the vigil going as the protestors took turns singing, chanting and preparing food for their colleagues.
Keen to keep public opinion on their side, the staff have also kept branches of Credit Foncier open for business.

While Arthuis has insisted that there will be no money from the government to revive the bank, his statements over recent days have become more nuanced as he argues that he is merely dealing with the only proposal available to him.

One of the most controversial issues, however, is that after a loss of nearly 11 billion francs ($2 billion) in 1995, which triggered the break-up plan, Meyssonnier himself has said the bank could make a profit this year of one billion francs this year.

Moreover, unions say the government, and in particular the Finance Ministry, is to blame for its misadventures in the property market in the 1980s, because the state was in charge of nominating top management and keeping tabs on the group's financial situation. ($1=5.500 French Franc)
